To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the majority of patients with supracondylar humerus fractures have a pulseless, pale, and paralysed hand.
the majority of children with a supracondylar humerus fracture have a pulseless hand and a normal arterial pressure, and that exploration of the bracchial artery is not indicated in these patients.
the incidence of vascular injury in supracondylar humeral fractures in children is low and that the risk of neurovascular complications is highest in children younger than 6 years.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the pink, pulseless, hand is a rare complication of supracondyl fracture; it is associated with a poor prognosis, and is best treated by early exploration of the bracchial artery, and of the nerves.

the brachial pulse is not an accurate guide to the presence or absence of arterial injury; the pulseless hand is a reliable sign of arterial injury; and that, in the majority of cases, the brachial arterial injury is not associated with nerve injury.

the pink, pulseless, hand is a true emergency and should be managed as such, with urgent exploration of the artery and the nerves, with the aim of achieving early restoration of the circulation to the hand and the restoration of the function of the nerves.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pink, pulseless, paralyzed hand in children is not a surgical emergency.
the pink pulseless hand is not always an indication for immediate exploration.
we found that the incidence of vascular injury in children with supracondylar humeral fractures was 1% and the incidence of neurologic injury was 5.3%.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the management of these fractures has changed dramatically in the last decade.
the majority of these injuries are amenable to a nonoperative management, with only 5–10% of patients requiring exploration.
, although it is not possible to identify the patients who will develop neurovascular complications, it is possible to identify those who are at high risk of developing them.
